# Kumbhakārajātaka (Ja 408)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Kumbhakārajātaka* (Ja 408), translated as *The Potter*, is a canonical verse narrative with prose commentary belonging to the Jātaka collection of the Khuddaka Nikāya [SuttaCentral; Wiltshire 1990]. The framed narrative is set at Jetavana, where the Buddha addresses the restraint of defilements (*kilesaniggaha*), connecting to background circumstances also presented in the *Pānīyajātaka* [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is born into a potter's family (*kumbhakārakula*) in a suburb of Bārāṇasī, earning a living to support his wife, son, and daughter [Fausböll 1883; Fenn 1994]. His wife takes the initiative to renounce worldly life first, departing through the back door and leaving the Bodhisatta to raise their children until they are independent; once they are self-sufficient, he also goes forth as an ascetic, attains meditative masteries (*jhānābhiññā*), and is reborn in the Brahma realm [Fausböll 1883; Emmanuel 2013; Fenn 1994]. In the closing identification (*samodhāna*), the potter is identified as the Buddha, his wife as Rāhulamātā, his son as Rāhula, and his daughter as Uppalavaṇṇā [Fausböll 1883].
A central component of the work is the integrated verse and prose legend of four kings who become solitary buddhas (*paccekabuddhas*) and inspire the Bodhisatta's renunciation [Wiltshire 1990; Fenn 1994]. Belonging to early ascetic poetry, the metrical portion includes a memorial *gāthā* providing the names and capitals of the four rulers, alongside four verses describing the visual signs or meditation subjects (*ārammaṇa*) that prompted their awakening [Norman 1983; Wiltshire 1990]. For instance, King Karaṇḍu of Kāliṅga is awakened by contemplating a mango tree plundered of its fruit in contrast with a barren, unmolested tree, while King Naggaji is awakened by observing the clashing and solitary stillness of bracelets on a woman's arm, an image also found in the *Khaggavisāṇa Sutta* [Wiltshire 1990; UNDV 2009].
The text shares direct thematic and metrical parallels with Jain literature, notably the *Uttarādhyayana Sūtra*, which preserves corresponding verses listing the same four kings, their cities, and the signs triggering their renunciation [Norman 1983; Samuel 2008]. Studies also note the transmission of the narrative into Central Asian traditions, including Uighur script [Yang 2013]. Internally, DharmaNexus records eight text-reuse matches between the canonical verses and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. Cross-tradition machine alignments also link passages of the text with Sanskrit recensions of the *Bhikṣuṇīvinaya* and the Tibetan translation of the *Pūrṇaparipṛcchāsūtra* [DharmaNexus].
